title: Who Gets the Desk? A Simulated Case Study of Unequal Access in Two School Districts · 独立口语迁移
instructions: 先完成示范段的跟读诊断，再用不同人物、信息或立场录制自己的完整回答。示范与自由回答分别取证，服务未提供完整听音评阅时保持待评。
reference: In the fictional coastal city of Marlow Bay, two school districts—Northbank and Southfield—serve families with very different resources. Northbank, in the wealthier hills, has three well-equipped primary schools. Southfield, near the industrial port, has one overcrowded primary school and a waiting list of 240 children. Last September, the city council published a report showing that Southfield’s classrooms held an average of 38 pupils, while Northbank’s held 22. The report also noted that Southfield had no library room and only one computer for every 15 students. Northbank had a library in each school and one computer for every 4 students. These numbers are simulated for this case study, but they reflect patterns found in many real cities where wealth and school quality are closely linked. The council did not ignore the gap. In October, it announced a “Fair Start” plan. The plan had three parts. First, the city would build two new classrooms at Southfield Primary by the following September.
prompt:
Part 1
Do you think all children should have the same school resources?
What can governments do to help schools in poor areas?
Have you ever seen a school with too many students in one class?
Is transport important for students to get to school?

Part 2
Describe a time when a school or a community tried to solve a problem of unequal access. You should say: what the problem was; who tried to solve it; what they did; and whether it worked.

Part 3
Why do some schools have more resources than others?
Should rich schools share their teachers with poor schools?
How can we measure whether a school is fair?
What is more important: more classrooms or better teachers?
